contributions.headingText: Granular cell tumour is a neuroectodermal neoplasm with Schwannian differentiation and is composed of epithelioid to polygonal cells with copious eosinophilic, distinctively granular cytoplasm.

Not recommended: granular cell schwannoma; granular cell nerve sheath tumour; granular cell myoblastoma; Abrikossoff tumour.

The vulva is the most common site of involvement within the female genital tract, with exceptional cases reported in the ovary, cervix, and vagina {8610749}. The labium majus is the most common location; rarely, mons pubis and clitoral involvement occur {17309466; 10785484; 29305965}. Synchronous or metachronous tumours are known to occur {20173503; 30166553; 32089415}.

Patients with granular cell tumours present with a slow-growing, mobile, non-tender, occasionally pruritic mass that is usually < 40 mm {24303488}. The overlying epidermis can be ulcerated, depigmented, or thickened with a cobblestone appearance {24303488; 20173503}.

This rare soft tissue tumour is in the majority of cases benign and can involve the female genital tract, often the vulva {24371657; 36595970}. These tumours can occur throughout the body and at any age. They occur more often in female individuals than in male individuals, and some studies have reported a higher frequency of occurrence in Black women and people in their fourth to sixth decades of life {22517025}. Paediatric vulvar granular cell tumours are exceedingly rare and have a median patient age of 8.5 years {29305965}.
Multiple granular cell tumours can arise in association with Noonan syndrome {11045593; 20537083; 18577039}.

Loss-of-function mutations affecting the V-ATPase accessory genes are found in 72% of granular cell tumours overall {30166553; 30597645}. These genes play pivotal roles in endosomal pH regulation. Loss-of-function mutations affecting these genes are found irrespective of anatomical site or whether the lesions are benign or malignant, and such mutations have only been rarely (< 0.1%) detected in common cancer types {30166553}.
Vulvar granular cell tumours are small, firm, frequently solitary, whitish nodules with well-defined borders involving dermis/submucosa or subcutis {10785484}.

Granular cell tumours have poorly defined borders and are composed of sheets, nests, and trabeculae of large, monotonous epithelioid to polygonal cells with intensely eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm. Cell borders may be indistinct, producing a syncytial appearance. Nuclei are usually centrally situated and range from uniformly small and mildly hyperchromatic to larger and vesicular with distinct nucleoli. Mitoses are variable in number but usually not prominent. The finely granular appearance of the cytoplasm is due to massive accumulation of lysosomes, including larger intracytoplasmic granules highlighted by clear haloes {17448196}. Perineural infiltration is common. Overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is sometimes seen and, when extensive, can raise the consideration of squamous cell carcinoma {20173503; 1848836}. Granular cell tumours are generally reactive for S100, SOX10, nestin, inhibin, and calretinin {16487364; 24746209}.

Malignant granular cell tumours are rare, accounting for approximately 2.5% of all cases {32089415; 36595970}. Necrosis and mitotic activity are considered the most reliable histological indicators of aggressive tumours; however, metastasis remains the most widely accepted definitive criterion for malignant granular cell tumours {32089415}. For detailed histological and immunohistochemical features and a description of the histological features associated with aggressive behaviour, see the Soft tissue and bone tumours volume [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Soft tissue and bone tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2020. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 3). https://publications.iarc.fr/588.]].
Loss-of-function mutations in ATP6AP1 or ATP6AP2 are helpful in supporting the diagnosis of granular cell tumour in morphologically difficult cases {30166553; 30597645}.

Essential: nests and trabeculae of large oval to round cells; abundant, intensely eosinophilic granular cytoplasm.

Desirable: S100 or SOX10 positivity by immunohistochemistry.

The prognostic utility of the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition TNM staging system for malignant granular cell tumours remains unproven, as clinical evidence supporting its effectiveness is currently lacking.

The majority of vulvar granular cell tumours and granular cell tumour at all sites are benign {20527248}. Malignant granular cell tumours are rare and typically exhibit an aggressive clinical course. For a detailed description of prognosis, see the WHO classification of tumours of soft tissue and bone [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Soft tissue and bone tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2020. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 3). https://publications.iarc.fr/588.]].
